title: Painting
short_answer: Protect, prep, prime every bare surface, then cut in and roll while wet. Paint reveals — it doesn't hide. Two coats means two coats.
summary: Paint doesn't hide anything. It reveals. Every hour of prep buys back more than an hour of paint, and no amount of good paint rescues bad preparation.
plain_words: Protect everything, clean everything, prime everything bare. Then cut in the edges and roll while the cut-in is still wet so it blends. Two coats means two coats — one heavy coat is not the same thing. Check the sheen on the drawings before you start, because the shinier the paint, the more it shows every flaw underneath it.
when_to_use: Production paint on new board after drywall finish and clean-out
Prime and finish coats per finish schedule and specification
Before punch — full-room or full-plane coating, not spot touch-up
prerequisites: Drywall finished to the specified GA-214 level
Room clean, dust-free, and conditions within product limits
Finish schedule: products, sheen, and coat count confirmed

tools.name: Brushes and rollers matched to prior application method
Roller covers in correct nap for texture
Vacuum and tack cloths for dust removal
Spray rig with masking and containment (when method is spray)
Humidity thermometer / moisture meter for conditions

materials.name: Primer matched to substrate (drywall, stain-blocking, bonding, block filler)
Finish paint per schedule — product, sheen, and batch
Masking tape, poly, and floor protection
Acoustic sealant or caulk where detail requires
Labeled leftover paint samples for future touch-up

steps.title: Protect
steps.body: Floors, glass, hardware, fixtures, casework, and anything already finished. The cheapest insurance on the job.

steps.title: Protect
steps.body: Mask rather than rely on a steady hand for anything that's expensive to fix.

steps.title: Protect
steps.body: Remove or mask hardware, plates, and covers instead of cutting around them.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Get the sanding dust off. Paint over drywall dust is an adhesion failure waiting to peel. Vacuum and wipe, don't just blow it around.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Walk it with a raking light and fix what you find now — see Drywall Touch-Up.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Caulk where the detail calls for it. Clean, tooled joints only.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Confirm temperature, humidity, and surface moisture are within the product's stated range. Cold or damp will cost you a coat.

steps.title: Prime
steps.body: New board always gets primed. Board face and joint compound absorb at different rates — without primer, every joint and every screw photographs through the finish coats.

steps.title: Prime
steps.body: Match the primer to the problem: drywall primer/sealer on new board, stain-blocking over water stains, marker, smoke or tannin, bonding primer over glossy or unknown coatings, block filler on CMU.

steps.title: Prime
steps.body: Spot-prime every repair, even small ones.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Cut in, then roll into the wet cut-in. If the cut-in dries first you get a visible band around the whole room.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Maintain a wet edge and work in manageable sections. Lap marks come from rolling into paint that's already setting.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Correct roller nap for the texture — too short starves it, too long stipples it.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Respect the spread rate on the can. Stretching coverage to save material costs you a third coat.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Full dry time between coats, not "it feels dry."

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: De-nib lightly between coats where needed.

steps.title: Finish coats
steps.body: Keep a labeled sample of every colour and product used — that's what makes future touch-up possible. See Paint Touch-Up.

warnings.title: The handoff that decides the whole job
warnings.body: The paint job is only as good as the drywall under it, and the drywall is only as good as the finish level that was specified. A Level 4 wall under semi-gloss paint in raking light will generate complaints that look like painting defects and aren't. See Finishing Drywall levels of finish. Catch that mismatch before the first coat, not after.

experts.summary: Sheen decides how forgiving the wall is: flat/matte hides flaws best but is hardest to clean; eggshell is the common commercial compromise; satin is more washable and less forgiving; semi-gloss and gloss are durable but show everything — every flaw, roller mark, and touch-up. If the finish schedule shows semi-gloss on a Level 4 wall, that's a conversation before anyone paints. Spray is fastest on open unoccupied space but overspray travels further than expected — containment and masking eat the gain. Backrolling (spray then immediately roll) works coating into the surface and evens texture — often right on new board. Rolling gives the most control and is usually correct in occupied buildings and tight spaces. Match the method between coats and between areas — a sprayed wall next to a rolled wall in the same colour reads as two different colours because the textures differ.

quality_checks.prompt: Substrate dust-free — vacuumed and wiped, not blown around
New board and every repair primed before finish coats
Sheen and finish level match spec — mismatch escalated before coating
Coat count, spread rate, and dry times per product data sheet
Labeled leftover paint retained for future touch-up

common_mistakes.title: Painting over dust
common_mistakes.right: Vacuum and wipe substrate before primer
common_mistakes.why: Adhesion failure that shows after handover

common_mistakes.title: Skipping primer on new board
common_mistakes.wrong: Finish directly on new board or repairs
common_mistakes.right: Drywall primer on all bare surfaces; spot-prime repairs
common_mistakes.why: Every joint and screw telegraphs through finish

common_mistakes.title: Sheen and finish-level mismatch
common_mistakes.wrong: Paint semi-gloss over Level 4 without escalation
common_mistakes.right: Match GA-214 level to sheen before first coat
common_mistakes.why: Complaints look like paint defects but are drywall scope

common_mistakes.title: Cut-in drying before roll
common_mistakes.wrong: Cut in entire room then roll hours later
common_mistakes.right: Roll into wet cut-in section by section

common_mistakes.title: Stretching spread rate
common_mistakes.why: Buys a third coat and uneven colour

common_mistakes.title: Recoating before dry
common_mistakes.wrong: Second coat when surface feels dry
common_mistakes.right: Full dry time per data sheet
common_mistakes.why: Failure shows later, not during application

common_mistakes.title: Inadequate protection
common_mistakes.wrong: Spray or roll without masking adjacent finishes
common_mistakes.right: Protect floors, glass, casework, and overspray paths
common_mistakes.why: Overspray and drips on someone else's work

common_mistakes.title: Mixing spray and roll in same field
common_mistakes.wrong: Spray one wall, roll the adjacent wall same colour
common_mistakes.right: Match method between coats and visible areas
common_mistakes.why: Different texture reads as two colours

common_mistakes.title: No labeled leftovers
common_mistakes.wrong: Finish job without retaining labeled paint
common_mistakes.right: Label and retain sample of every colour and product
common_mistakes.why: Every future touch-up starts wrong without the right can

provenance.note: Sequence, primer selection, wet-edge and cut-in practice, and sheen behaviour follow paint manufacturer application guidance and standard commercial painting practice. Products, spread rates, dry and recoat times, and temperature and humidity limits are product-specific from the data sheet for the actual specified coating — those numbers are never carried between products. The finish-level and sheen interaction is documented in Finishing Drywall; the flashing mechanism behind the priming requirement is in Paint Touch-Up.
